subject.title: A Poem for the Old Man
subject.author: John Wieners
subject.text:
God love you
   Dana my lover
lost in the horde
on this Friday night,
500 men are moving up
& down from the bath
room to the bar.
Remove this desire
from the man I love.
Who has opened
   the savagery
of the sea to me.
 
See to it that
his wants are filled
on California street
Bestow on him lar-
gesse that allows him
peace in his loins.
 
Leave him not
to the moths.
Make him out a lion
so that all who see him
hero worship his
thick chest as I did
moving my mouth
over his back bringing
our hearts to heights
I never hike over
   anymore.
Let blond hair burn
on the back of his
neck, let no ache
screw his face
up in pain, his soul
   is so hooked.
Not heroin.
Rather fix these
hundred men as his
lovers & lift him
with the enormous bale
of their desire.
 
6.20.58

title: The Prayer That Multiplies What It Should Cure
standfirst: Written in a San Francisco flophouse days after his six-year relationship finally ended, John Wieners's poem borrows the exact shape of a Catholic intercession — then uses it to ask God for the one thing that kind of prayer is supposed to talk you out of.

sections.heading: A Printer Who Wouldn't Set the Words
sections.body:
In June 1958, a Kansan just out of the Army named David Haselwood was starting a small press in San Francisco's North Beach, and he had no name for it yet beyond an idea. The book that became Auerhahn Press's first title was a slim manuscript by a twenty-four-year-old poet, John Wieners: *The Hotel Wentley Poems*. Haselwood took the pages to a commercial printer, and the printer set the type with the sequence's rougher words missing, [the spaces simply left blank](https://fromasecretlocation.com/auerhahn-press/). Haselwood was angry enough about it that he taught himself typesetting and bought his own letterpress, so that no jobbing printer would ever again get to decide what one of his poets' lines was allowed to say.

*A Poem for the Old Man*, dated in the poet's own hand "6.20.58," belongs to that same small book, written in that same fraught month. It names five hundred men circulating between a bar and its bathroom, and a lover's chest, mouth and loins — content frank enough for 1958. But no printer would have known to blank any of it, because none of it arrives as profanity. It arrives as a prayer.

sections.heading: The Shape of a Petition, Filled With the Wrong Wish
sections.body:
Read the grammar rather than the images and the poem is unmistakably liturgical. It opens on direct address — "God love you" — then runs through a string of imperatives aimed, over the reader's shoulder, at that same God: see to it that, bestow on him, leave him not, make him out, let no ache. That is the architecture of an intercession, the kind of prayer a Catholic-school boy is taught to say on someone else's behalf, asking for their protection or their deliverance from temptation.

Wieners had exactly that schooling — Boston College High School, then Boston College itself, both run by Jesuits — and he uses the form with total fluency while turning its content upside down. The poem's first actual request does ask God to "remove this desire / from the man I love," but everything after it contradicts that plea: not less wanting for Dana, but more — his wants filled, largesse bestowed, and by the final stanza an outright multiplication, "these / hundred men as his / lovers." The poem doesn't ask God to cure Dana of desire. It asks God to supply him with an abundance of it, and calls that mercy.

Wieners does this elsewhere in the same small book. In "A Poem for Cocksuckers," he addresses "Mary in our hour of / despair" and pleads, "Take not / away from me the small fires / I burn in the memory of love" — the vocabulary of the rosary borrowed for exactly what the rosary was built to discourage. [Reviewing his collected work decades later](https://www.bookforum.com/print/2204/john-wieners-s-poems-join-the-sacred-and-the-profane-15258), the critic Albert Mobilio named this Wieners's signature move: "heroin, bulging cocks, and pleas to God mix freely together," he wrote, "all suffused with a profound sense of divine grace."

sections.heading: Six Years, Two Cities, and a Last Week in a Borrowed Room
sections.body:
The "old man" of the title is a joke at Dana Durkee's expense — he had just turned twenty-nine, five years older than Wieners, which was apparently enough of a gap between two men in their twenties to earn the name. Durkee was a former high-school football player from Swampscott who'd spent four years in the Navy before coming home to Boston and training as a fireman; Wieners, [by one recent account of the relationship](https://glreview.org/article/a%E2%80%88poet-with-the-angst-of-the-age/), fell for him in 1952, and the two spent six on-and-off years together, sharing a run of Beacon Hill apartments a short walk from where Wieners would eventually live for the last thirty years of his life.

Durkee stayed in Boston working while Wieners went to study at Black Mountain College in 1955 and 1956; by [one account of those years](https://www.elisarolle.com/queerplaces/pqrst/Russell%20Dana%20Durkee.html), he went partly to be near Durkee's wider circle and pined for him from North Carolina rather than getting over him. In the fall of 1957 the two finally moved to San Francisco together, to [North Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Beach,_San_Francisco), where Wieners fell in with the city's poets and painters. It was there, not in Boston, that the relationship ended for the last time. With nowhere fixed to live, Wieners moved between friends' couches, and in a borrowed room at the Hotel Wentley, in the [Polk Gulch bathhouse district](https://ultrawolvesunderthefullmoon.blog/2022/11/22/john-wieners-the-savagerey-of-the-sea/), he wrote, across six days that June, the sequence that became his first book.

The date at the foot of the poem is precise enough to check against a calendar: 20 June 1958 was in fact a Friday, the same night the poem itself names — a small, verifiable seam between what a poet wrote and what actually happened that week, in a poem that otherwise reads like an invocation rather than a diary entry.

sections.heading: The Word He Catches Himself Using
sections.body:
Deep in the poem's last movement, asking God to spare Dana any pain, Wieners writes: "his soul / is so hooked. / Not heroin." It's a strange thing to specify. Nothing before that line has mentioned drugs; the poem has been an argument about desire, not addiction. But the denial only makes sense as a denial if the word "hooked" had already started, in the world Wieners was writing from, to carry both meanings at once — desire and dependency running so close along the same nerve that a poet reaching for one has to wave off the other.

*The Hotel Wentley Poems* was written the same year as Allen Ginsberg's *Howl*, Frank O'Hara's *Meditations in an Emergency*, and Jack Spicer's *After Lorca* — [a cluster of books](https://electricliterature.com/the-purity-of-something-i-do-not-know-on-john-wienerss-selected-poems-and-selected-journals/) by poets for whom the line between erotic compulsion and chemical compulsion was rarely a clean one. Wieners's own life went on to blur it further, if not always in the specific way he'd just disclaimed. What actually recurred was psychiatric hospitalization: [Medfield State for six months](https://www.thenation.com/article/culture/john-wieners-letters-essay/) beginning in 1959, Metropolitan State in 1961, where ninety-one insulin shock treatments produced what he later called his "forgotten year," then Central Islip in 1969 and Taunton in 1972. "Hooked" turned out to be the right word for the next four decades of his life. It just attached itself to a different noun than the one he'd ruled out.

sections.heading: The Book Almost No One Could Buy, and the Poet Who Vouched for It Anyway
sections.body:
Frank O'Hara admired *The Hotel Wentley Poems* enough to put his opinion of it inside one of his own poems, wondering aloud whether the book was as great as he'd been telling people — then [answering himself](https://electricliterature.com/the-purity-of-something-i-do-not-know-on-john-wienerss-selected-poems-and-selected-journals/): it was. Allen Ginsberg went further, [calling Wieners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wieners) "one of the greatest poets around, or, certainly, the most Romantic, and doomed, poet around." Two of the best-connected poets of the twentieth century, saying in print that this small book mattered.

It still spent decades hard to find. Copyright tangles kept it out of print at a stretch; [one professor](https://electricliterature.com/the-purity-of-something-i-do-not-know-on-john-wienerss-selected-poems-and-selected-journals/) teaching it to graduate students had to track down bootleg chapbook copies run off by a small outfit called Joy Street Press — the same Joy Street, on Beacon Hill, where Wieners himself lived for thirty years, a coincidence of naming that neither he nor his students seem to have remarked on. By his own late reckoning and [that of critics writing after his death](https://www.thenation.com/article/culture/john-wieners-letters-essay/), Wieners spent most of those decades close to invisible in American poetry: read with devotion by other poets, largely absent from anyone else's shelf. Only in this century — a selected poems in 2015, a collected letters in 2021 — has that started to change.

Dana Durkee, for what it's worth, did not get the hundred lovers the poem asked God to send him. [By the record that survives](https://www.elisarolle.com/queerplaces/pqrst/Russell%20Dana%20Durkee.html), he married a woman, Patricia Fielder, in 1966, and that marriage is the last fact anyone seems to have thought worth writing down about him. The prayer wasn't answered on its own terms. It just outlived the two men it was about — which is not nothing, for a poem, and rather more than most prayers manage.
